title: Will AI make dental professionals less expert?
html:
‘If the answer is AI, what’s the question?’ Dr Nicola Millard has spent much of her career trying to stop organisations from getting that order wrong.

A social scientist and technologist, Millard is principal innovation partner at BT Group and holds a PhD in technology acceptance. She began working with artificial intelligence (AI) in the 1990s, applying neural networks to BT’s call centres, and has since become a leading voice on how technology changes customer experience and working life. She has written more than 50 publications and delivered two TEDx talks.

In this episode of Dentistry Talks, Millard turns her attention to AI in dentistry. The technology may save time, but could it also weaken clinical skills and leave dental teams handling only the most difficult work?

She points to radiology, where AI can interpret X-rays with impressive accuracy. Pairing an experienced clinician with the technology can produce strong results. However, research suggests that when the AI is removed, the clinician can become less expert.

‘We kind of do need to keep our brain, kind of like a muscle,’ Millard says. ‘We need to keep that muscle well toned and not rely too much on the AI.’

Does AI have the required dental expertise?

If technology handles more routine interpretation, less experienced professionals may struggle to develop the judgement required to recognise when it is wrong. Because, as we all know, generative AI can present false information with confidence.

‘It makes stuff up. It looks very convincing,’ Millard says. ‘We’ve kind of digitised mansplaining at this point.’

She argues that organisations should move beyond keeping a ‘human in the loop’. The human needs to remain ‘in the lead’, with the knowledge and authority to challenge an automated recommendation.

Millard also questions whether technology will give dental professionals more time. Previous innovations have often intensified work instead. Once straightforward tasks are automated, teams may be left with a relentless stream of complex decisions and emotionally demanding interactions.

From rogue chatbots and patient data to AI burnout and agent-led appointment booking, this episode asks how dentistry can use artificial intelligence without surrendering expertise, trust or control.

You can now watch the full episode on YouTube or listen on Spotify.

Topics include:

  • Whether AI could weaken clinical expertise
  • Artificial intelligence in dental diagnostics and radiology
  • Why humans should remain ‘in the lead’
  • Hallucinations, rogue chatbots and accountability
  • Patient data, cybersecurity and trust
  • The ‘useful, usable and used’ test for dental technology
  • AI burnout and the intensification of dental work
  • How artificial intelligence could change patient appointments
  • Preparing dental students and teams to work with AI.
